input.rationale: Review of the second-scenario direct check 5a560c55 (unit-claim-install-snapshot-alignment), whose fresh execution b9d811ad439049be9c19247ec7db97b2 completed the comparison with the declarative prerequisite matched, comparison_complete and witness_complete true, and the assertion violated: after the install retained a tail (node_last_index 5, term 1, tail_retained true), the AppendEntries a leader sends next - anchored at the snapshot index - was rejected (append_success false, tail_replaced false, last entry unchanged). This is a second violated scenario of the same requirement and a sharper one than the first: the misalignment does not only misreport the last entry, it stops the follower accepting the leader's entries. This review supplies the required checker_correspondence item and re-resolves the claim-level applicability issue, which is open again for this artifact because a resolution answers its own lineage.

review_items.rationale: Requirement versus encoded predicate: the obligation requires the receiver to align its log with the installed snapshot so its last entry does not come from an unconfirmed branch, and this scenario encodes the operational consequence of getting that wrong - the AppendEntries a leader sends after a successful install (nextIndex = snapshot index + 1, hence anchored at the snapshot index) must be accepted. S57 shows the receive path adopting the snapshot index and compacting without setting the last log, S58 shows the compaction removes entries through the snapshot index, S54 shows the effective last entry is the maximum of log and snapshot position so the anchor is no longer the last entry once a tail survives, and S8 shows that the previous-log check then falls through to the log store and rejects with NoRetryBackoff. Entry and caller duties: the harness declares the retained tail from the install event, anchors the request at the installed index with a conflicting term, and delivers it through the production handler. Identity: op_id tail-1 appears on both the install event and the append event, and the prerequisite correlation matched. Oracle: acceptance and the resulting last entry are read from emitted fields, not tests_passed; the run exited 0 while the anchor was rejected, which is the case this oracle must catch. Observation path and completion: the install response and the append response were both received, and the run completed. Counterevidence: none of the open issues is evidence against the encoded predicate; the protocol-alignment reading and the adaptations are recorded below.
limitations: The retained-tail state was seeded through the caller-owned log store rather than produced by a real leader's snapshot decision, so reachability under a leader remains a premise.

Node goroutines were disabled and a substitute answered restore futures; the check isolates the two handlers' decisions and does not exercise FSM restore, the main loop or the leader's subsequent nextIndex walk.
The check reports the receiver's rejection only: whether the leader then decrements nextIndex and re-sends a snapshot (and how long that loop lasts) was not measured.

conf.TrailingLogs was 0 so compaction ran at the snapshot index; with the default the trailing-log guard would have skipped compaction entirely and the anchor would have remained in the log, which is a different starting state and is not covered here.

review_items.rationale: The antecedent is declared before the result: the install event reports the retained tail from the handler's own bookkeeping, and the appended request is anchored at the installed index, which is the position a leader uses after a successful install. Nothing was filtered by the observed rejection, and no applicability condition depends on append_success. The claim-level condition concerns whether a later AppendEntries is an acceptable substitute for aligning at install time, which is the reading the claim addresses rather than a precondition for whether the requirement applies to this receiver.
limitations: One carrier, one installed index and one tail shape; other index/tail combinations are not covered.
Real-leader reachability and the leader's follow-up behaviour remain open.

condition_dispositions.rationale: Whether relying on the next AppendEntries is acceptable in every deployment is a separate question from whether the receiver owes alignment at install time; the second scenario measures the consequence of that reliance but does not depend on how it is characterised, and the boundary is carried in this review's limitations.

resolutions.rationale: This is the claim-level record of the snapshot-protocol conflict, open again here because a resolution answers the artifact it was written against. The answer is the same attributed reading, now sharpened by a second executed scenario: the protocol requires a receiver that cannot confirm the snapshot's last included entry to discard the log, the implementation leaves that removal to a later AppendEntries (S57, S58), and the second scenario shows why the deferral matters - with a retained tail the anchor index is no longer the effective last entry (S54), so the very AppendEntries that was supposed to perform the removal is rejected (S8) and the tail survives. The claim therefore asserts the install-time alignment duty, and the question of whether the deferral is nevertheless harmless in a deployment is retained as an outer boundary.
scope_limitations: Whether a real leader drives a follower into the retained-tail state, and how long the resulting rejection lasts, remain open outside this claim.

findings.description: Confirmed violation of: For every FSM that implements ConfigurationStore, the library must invoke StoreConfiguration(index, configuration) for each committed configuration log entry that it delivers to the FSM, so that a persistent FSM can reconstruct configuration without an external snapshot.

Confirmed violation of: Every AppendEntries RPC a server processes, including a pure heartbeat handled by the transport fast path, is subject to the same RPC-header compatibility check that the normal RPC path applies before appendEntries, so a peer outside the supported protocol-version window cannot step the server down, advance its persisted term, be adopted as the known leader or refresh its last contact.

Confirmed violation of: A TimeoutNow request is honoured only when its sender is attributed to the receiver's authority context, at minimum a voter of the receiver's latest configuration, so that a peer outside that configuration cannot clear the receiver's known leader, force it into candidate state and hand it the transfer privilege that skips pre-vote and makes other voters grant votes despite having a leader.

Confirmed violation of: On a successful InstallSnapshot at index N, a receiver that no longer holds a log entry at N matching the snapshot's last included term must discard the log entries above N, so that its effective last entry and its later vote comparisons and replication decisions are not based on a branch the snapshot did not confirm.

Measured violation awaiting attribution: Direct oracle correspondence is unreviewed; Open review issue 7bcba806871948e49b8891aa6bd2c2b7 [S57,S58,S54,S8]: The snapshot protocol requires discarding the log whenever the receiver cannot confirm the snapshot's last included entry, while this implementation relies on a later AppendEntries to truncate the tail.

assumptions: The entry has been committed (reached the FSM via processLogs).
The FSM implements ConfigurationStore as documented in configuration.go:44-52.

units.rationale: First Candidate, grounded on the accepted map. Reading the previously unmapped FSM/apply path (fsm.go) surfaced a sourced discrepancy: ConfigurationStore documents that StoreConfiguration is invoked once a configuration log entry is committed (configuration.go:38-52), but the only call site is inside applySingle, and runFSM calls applySingle only when the FSM does NOT implement BatchingFSM (fsm.go:127-186). Separately, BatchingFSM.ApplyBatch documents that LogConfiguration entries 'will be sent' to the batching FSM (fsm.go:51-69). A FSM that implements both interfaces therefore never receives StoreConfiguration, and the configuration fact is established for it only by whatever its own ApplyBatch chooses to do. The library's own test helper (testing_batch.go:13-33) implements ApplyBatch under the batchtest build flag and simply returns nil for non-LogCommand entries, which is consistent with the discrepancy rather than with the ConfigurationStore contract. This product therefore fixes the responsibility, the attribution and a bounded discriminator; construction of the formal check is deferred to the next turn. The map is extended with the behavior and fact that support this question (b-fsm-apply-committed, f-fsm-configuration-state); no previously accepted object is modified or removed.

audit_question.question: When a FSM implements both BatchingFSM and ConfigurationStore, does the library invoke StoreConfiguration(index, configuration) for a committed LogConfiguration entry, as the ConfigurationStore contract states, or does the batching dispatch in runFSM make that invocation unreachable?
audit_question.importance: ConfigurationStore exists so a persistent FSM can treat its own state as a complete snapshot and recover without an external snapshot (configuration.go:44-52). If the invocation is unreachable for batching FSMs, an application that implements both interfaces silently loses the only library-provided delivery of committed configuration changes, which matters for recovery and for the FSM's own view of cluster membership. This is an implementation/contract gap, not a consensus-safety violation; it is classified implementation_semantics.
contexts: committed LogConfiguration entry applied after a membership change
batched commit delivery when the FSM implements BatchingFSM
event_paths: AddVoter/RemoveServer -> appendConfigurationEntry -> dispatchLogs -> commit -> processLogs -> fsmMutateCh -> applyBatch
AddVoter/RemoveServer -> appendConfigurationEntry -> dispatchLogs -> commit -> processLogs -> fsmMutateCh -> applySingle -> StoreConfiguration

supporting_behavior_ids.b-append-entries-sync: A1 relationship: the configuration fact consumed during AppendEntries processing is the same configuration whose FSM-side persistence this question investigates; the FSM record is an alternative establishment path for the context that determines voter eligibility and therefore qualified support for advancement.
supporting_behavior_ids.b-recover-from-disk: Explains why the missing delivery matters: the FSM configuration record is the recovery substitute for an external snapshot.
supporting_behavior_ids.b-config-change: Establishes which LogConfiguration entries are committed and therefore owed to the FSM.

counterevidence: The early return at fsm.go:111-115 is explicitly commented as 'Return early to avoid incrementing the index and term for an unimplemented operation', showing the author considered the non-ConfigurationStore case deliberately.

BatchingFSM.ApplyBatch's own doc says LogConfiguration entries will be sent to the batching FSM, which is consistent with the batching FSM being expected to persist configuration itself; this may mean ConfigurationStore is intended to be a non-batching-only interface and the interface comment is merely imprecise.
No existing test in the snapshot combines BatchingFSM with ConfigurationStore, so the current behaviour is not contradicted by a failing retained expectation.
unknowns: Whether a FSM implementing both BatchingFSM and ConfigurationStore is a supported/legal configuration, or whether the two interfaces are contractually exclusive.
Whether the intended delivery point for batching FSMs is ApplyBatch alone, making the ConfigurationStore comment inaccurate rather than the dispatch incomplete.
Whether any library-owned or documented FSM (e.g. middleware examples) implements both interfaces and depends on StoreConfiguration.
audit_question.trigger_rationale: The map's A5/A6 surfaces for runFSM were unread; reading them showed that the batching path selects applyBatch instead of applySingle, and StoreConfiguration has exactly one call site (fsm.go:118) inside applySingle. The two interface doc comments cannot both hold for a FSM implementing both interfaces, which is a concrete sourced discrepancy rather than a generic untested case.

audit_question.question: Does the heartbeat fast path apply the RPC-header compatibility gate that the normal AppendEntries path applies, so that a peer whose RPCHeader.ProtocolVersion is outside the window checkRPCHeader accepts cannot step this server down, advance its persisted term, be adopted as known leader and refresh its last contact?
audit_question.importance: The header gate is the only guard that keeps a server from participating with a peer outside its supported protocol-version window. On the fast path a pure heartbeat still reaches appendEntries, which can persist a newer term, transition the receiver out of candidate/leader state, record the sender as the known leader and refresh lastContact. If an out-of-window peer can reach that path, this server can be held out of its own elections by a peer whose RPCs the same process rejects on every other route, which is an availability consequence on a core formation path; the guard asymmetry itself is an implementation-semantics concern.

RPC header outside the supported protocol-version window
single node with a Transport that implements the fast path
event_paths: peer -> net_transport decode -> heartbeat classification -> heartbeatFn -> processHeartbeat -> appendEntries (no checkRPCHeader)
peer -> net_transport decode -> consumeCh -> processRPC -> checkRPCHeader -> appendEntries (rejected when out of window)

supporting_behavior_ids.b-term-authority: Explains the A2 consequence of the missing gate: the receiver's context is changed by the bypass (step-down and persisted term) without the compatibility decision the other route makes.

The fast path only carries pure heartbeats and performs no log matching or commit propagation, so any consequence is confined to term, state, leader identity and last contact rather than to log safety.

No comment on processHeartbeat or on the transport fast path states that the header gate is intentionally skipped, but the fast path was introduced as a head-of-line-blocking optimisation (Transport.SetHeartbeatHandler doc) and may assume already-validated peers.

Whether the consequence on elections is observable: does a bypassing peer's heartbeat refresh lastContact often enough to keep the receiver from starting its own election.
Whether the asymmetry is deliberate, making the correct disposition a documented assumption rather than an obligation.
audit_question.trigger_rationale: Reading the previously deferred transport surfaces produced a concrete sourced asymmetry rather than a generic untested case: processRPC calls checkRPCHeader before appendEntries (S41, S42), while processHeartbeat calls appendEntries directly (S40) and is installed as the transport fast path for every pure AppendEntries heartbeat (S16, S43). The next action distinguishes whether this is an unintended omission or deliberate design, and whether the bypassing peer can exist in a legal deployment.

scope.description: A Raft node receiving a TimeoutNow request from a peer whose RPC header passes the version window. The obligation concerns the attribution required before the receiver abandons its leader context and raises the transfer privilege, not the election mechanics that follow.
assumptions: The receiver already knows a leader or is otherwise eligible to be asked to campaign.

units.rationale: Third candidate, grounded on the accepted map. The TimeoutNow receive handler is the only route that grants the vote-while-a-leader-exists privilege, and it validates nothing beyond the RPC-header version window - it cannot even check currency, because the request carries no term. By contrast requestVote and requestPreVote reject senders outside the configuration, and leadership grants votes despite a leader only when the privilege is set. The claim fixes the attribution responsibility without asserting a violation; reachability by a non-member, the consequence on a healthy leader, and the possibility that the design deliberately trusts leader discipline are all recorded as counterevidence and unknowns. The map gains behavior b-timeout-now and fact f-leader-transfer-privilege, with a new consumer edge on b-vote-campaign; no accepted object's meaning, identity or existing edges change.

audit_question.question: Is a TimeoutNow request honoured only when its sender is attributed to the receiver's authority context - a voter of the receiver's latest configuration - or can any peer whose RPC header passes the version window make the receiver clear its known leader, enter candidate state and receive the transfer privilege that skips pre-vote and makes peers vote despite having a leader?
audit_question.importance: TimeoutNow is the only route that grants the vote-while-a-leader-exists privilege; the code's own comment says that privilege 'could be abused otherwise' and defends it only by clearing the flag after each election. The receive handler (S49) checks nothing: the request carries only an RPCHeader with no term (S48), and the handler clears the leader, sets Candidate and raises the privilege before a single validation. The vote RPCs by contrast reject a candidate that is not in the configuration and are granted despite a leader only when that privilege is set (S6, S21). If a node that is not a member of the receiver's configuration can reach this handler - a removed server or a stale node still running the same protocol version - it can force term inflation and an election that peers will vote for, which is an authority-transition defect on a core path.
participants: voters that would grant the resulting vote requests
contexts: a peer whose RPC header is within the supported protocol window but is not a voter of the receiver's latest configuration
a receiver that currently has a known leader
event_paths: receiver -> runCandidate (pre-vote skipped) -> electSelf with LeadershipTransfer=true -> peers grant despite a leader

supporting_behavior_ids.b-vote-campaign: Shows what the privilege does: the campaign skips pre-vote and marks its RequestVote as a leadership transfer (S51).
supporting_behavior_ids.b-vote-grant: Shows the other half of the privilege: a voter grants despite a known leader when LeadershipTransfer is set (S6), so the receiver's election is winnable against an established leader.
supporting_behavior_ids.b-leadership-transfer: The legitimate producer of TimeoutNow, which shows the intended authority of the sender and is the contract the receive side does not enforce.

counterevidence: The RPC-header version window is still enforced on this path (S50), so a peer speaking an unsupported protocol version is rejected.
Only a leader drives leadershipTransfer, so under a correct CFT deployment the sender is the current leader; the handler may be relying on that rather than validating it.
The receiver cannot check currency even if it wanted to, because TimeoutNowRequest carries no term (S48); the missing validation may be a design consequence rather than an oversight.

The API doc for LeadershipTransfer states that using transfer leadership is safe in a mixed-version cluster and that an unpromotable follower fails gracefully, which suggests deliberate leniency on the receive side.
unknowns: Whether a peer that is not a voter of the receiver's latest configuration can reach timeoutNow in a legal deployment.
Whether the resulting term inflation or election can unseat a healthy leader rather than merely perturbing terms.
Whether the intended contract is that the receive side trusts the transport/leader discipline, making the correct disposition a documented assumption instead of a duty.
audit_question.trigger_rationale: Reading the leadership-transfer target selection and TimeoutNow wiring exposed a concrete asymmetry rather than a generic untested case: requestVote and requestPreVote both gate on configuration membership (S6, S21), while timeoutNow gates on nothing and the request has no term with which a receiver could check currency (S48, S49). The next action distinguishes whether this is reachable by a non-member in a legal deployment and whether an attributed obligation follows.

audit_question.question: After a successful InstallSnapshot at index N, does the receiver discard the log entries it cannot reconcile with the snapshot - so that its effective last entry never comes from a branch the snapshot did not confirm - or does it retain and report a tail above N even when it no longer holds an entry at N matching the snapshot's term?
audit_question.importance: The receiver's last log entry is what it advertises in RequestVote and what it uses for its own vote comparisons, and the AppendEntries success rule is what lets a leader count it towards a quorum. If a receiver installs a snapshot at N while keeping entries above N that the snapshot's history did not confirm, then until the next matching AppendEntries arrives the node votes and is counted on a log position that no longer describes its state; a candidate elected on that position would have to be brought back by a snapshot. The Raft snapshot protocol requires discarding the log in exactly this case, so the duty is well grounded rather than a stylistic preference.
participants: the receiver's log store and FSM
contexts: a receiver whose log holds entries above the snapshot index
a snapshot whose last included entry the receiver no longer holds
event_paths: leader -> InstallSnapshot -> installSnapshot -> snapshot restore -> compaction up to N -> response success
later leader -> AppendEntries with prevLogEntry N -> conflict truncation -> setLastLog

supporting_behavior_ids.b-append-entries-sync: The only later place the tail is removed, via conflict truncation followed by setLastLog.
supporting_behavior_ids.b-replication-recovery: The leader-side counterpart that decides to send a snapshot instead of entries.
supporting_behavior_ids.b-stable-position-reconstruction: Explains why the retained tail is visible at all: the effective last entry is the maximum of log and snapshot position.

counterevidence: The retained tail may be harmless in practice because the leader's next AppendEntries starts at N+1 and truncates on term mismatch, so the window can be short.
The observable local run used a single node with no leader traffic, so it shows the state rather than how long it persists or what the next AppendEntries does.
The library may rely on the transport and the leader to re-drive replication immediately, treating the state as transient rather than as a retained branch.
unknowns: Whether a receiver can actually be driven into that state by a real leader (the leader sends a snapshot when its own log no longer covers the follower's nextIndex, and a longer divergent follower log can reach it, but the exact sequence is not established).
Whether the window is ever long enough for a vote comparison or an election to depend on it.
Whether the intended design is that the tail is always transient.
audit_question.trigger_rationale: Reading the snapshot receive path after recording the log/snapshot position mechanism produced a concrete sourced difference rather than an untested case: installSnapshot updates lastApplied and lastSnapshot and compacts only up to the snapshot index (S57, S58), never calls setLastLog, and the effective last entry is the maximum of log and snapshot position (S54) while the only later truncation lives in appendEntries (S8). A direct local run of the receive path confirmed the retained tail, so the question is which responsibility the receiver owes at that moment, not whether the state exists.

First, partial-but-usable core map for the hashicorp/raft snapshot (module github.com/hashicorp/raft, commit c0dc6a0b). The submission records the two core relationships required by the activity roles and, crucially, their connection, from read code plus the membership design document: (A1) qualified support for decision formation and legal advancement, realized as pre-vote campaign -> real vote campaign -> per-term vote grants -> leader no-op + replication -> quorum commitment at or above the first index of the leader's term; and (A2) context validity and acquisition/transfer/loss of authority, realized as the durable current term plus per-term vote, step-down-and-bump on newer terms, and leadership transfer via TimeoutNow with the candidateFromLeadershipTransfer exemption. The connection is sourced: formation eligibility and the commitment quorum are read from the latest configuration; configuration changes are only opened once latest==committed and the leader has committed an entry of its own term (configurationChangeChIfStable), which is why a no-op is always dispatched on election; and old work is bounded by present authority (votes honoured only for their own term, an AppendEntries reply reporting a newer term driving handleStaleTerm/step-down, conflicting-suffix truncation rolling latest back to committed, and inflight futures failed with ErrLeadershipLost on step-down). Residual local anomalies are recorded under core_overview.open_details rather than blocking the overview: the appendEntries StoreLogs-failure TODO leaving lastLog stale (raft.go:1541), electSelf returning a nil response channel on self-vote persistence failure (raft.go:2023), and checkLeaderLease assuming a replState entry exists for every latest-config voter (raft.go:1054). Several high-consequence paths remain explicitly unmapped surfaces (installSnapshot body, leader-side snapshot shipping, runFSM, snapshot lifecycle), and the next step is to read them and pick a sourced discriminator rather than to treat this map as coverage. No obligation or check is claimed here.

after.purpose: Qualified support for decision formation and legal advancement: elect a leader and extend/commit the replicated log.
after.realization_summary: A candidate runs a pre-vote campaign (preElectSelf) that does not change its term and, on winning it, a real campaign (electSelf) that increments and persists the term and asks voters for a vote. Followers decide the vote in requestVote/requestPreVote with leader-stickiness, log up-to-date and one-vote-per-term guards. The elected leader dispatches a no-op for its term, replicates to each peer (followerReplication), and advances the commit index through the commitment struct once a quorum's matchIndex reaches at least the first entry of the leader's own term.
variants: pre-vote disabled falls back to electSelf directly
leadership-transfer candidate skips pre-vote
unknowns: Behaviour of the pipeline replication fast path under partial responses was only skimmed.

after.purpose: Context validity and acquisition, transfer or loss of authority: term ownership, state transitions, and leadership transfer.
after.realization_summary: Authority is the persisted current term plus the per-term vote. setCurrentTerm persists the term before exposing it; setState clears the known leader on every transition. A newer term observed in a vote request or AppendEntries forces a step-down and term update. leadershipTransfer pre-replicates to the target then sends TimeoutNow; the target sets candidateFromLeadershipTransfer and runs an election without pre-vote, and the flag is reset after each candidate run.

unknowns: Authority effects of leadership transfer when the target never wins were not fully traced.

A new change may only be accepted once latestIndex==committedIndex and the leader has committed an entry in its term.

formation.explanation: A follower whose heartbeat timer expires while it is an eligible voter transitions to Candidate and runCandidate starts a pre-vote campaign (preElectSelf) that proposes currentTerm+1 without touching the term. Each other voter answers in requestPreVote with the leader-stickiness, membership and log-up-to-date guards and without persisting anything. If a quorum of pre-votes is granted the candidate runs electSelf, which persists the new term and a self-vote, then requests votes; voters persist the vote in requestVote subject to the same guards plus one-vote-per-term. The first tally to reach quorumSize() sets the candidate to Leader. The leader then appends a no-op for its term and replicates; the commitment struct advances commitIndex only when an actual quorum's matchIndex reaches at least startIndex, the first index of the leader's own term.

context.explanation: Authority is the durable current term plus the durable per-term vote; there is no global leader identity. setCurrentTerm persists a term before it is exposed and setState clears the known leader on every transition. A newer term seen in RequestVote or AppendEntries forces a step-down and term update, so context is lost by observation, not by a clock. Leadership transfer pre-replicates to the target and sends TimeoutNow; the target marks candidateFromLeadershipTransfer so that it skips pre-vote and is not stepped down by an equal-term AppendEntries from the outgoing leader, and the flag is cleared after the candidate run. The configuration context is the pair (latest, committed); latest is in effect from the moment its entry is appended.

connection.explanation: The two lines meet in three places. (1) Eligibility for formation is read from the configuration context: only voters of the latest configuration are asked for votes and only their match indexes count for commitment, and the commitment struct is rebuilt from the configuration at leader setup and at each configuration change. (2) The leader's advancement duty is gated by its term context: configurationChangeChIfStable is only non-nil once latest==committed and the leader has committed an entry of its own term (commitIndex >= startIndex), which is why a no-op is dispatched on election even with no client work. (3) Old work is bounded by present authority: a persisted vote is only honoured for its own term, an AppendEntries reply that reports a newer term drives handleStaleTerm and a step-down, a conflicting suffix truncation rolls latest back to committed, and on step-down the leader fails all inflight log futures with ErrLeadershipLost while replication goroutines are stopped.

open_details: appendEntries has an explicit TODO (raft.go:1541): if StoreLogs fails after a truncation, lastLog is left stale. Whether any real store can fail there, and its consequence, is unresolved.
electSelf returns a nil response channel when persisting the self-vote fails (raft.go:2023), leaving the candidate to wait out its election timer; this is a storage-failure path only.

checkLeaderLease assumes leaderState.replState contains every voter of the latest configuration (raft.go:1054); ordering on the main thread appears to guarantee this, but a nil-map lookup would panic and was not tested.

The pre-vote path treats a transport 'unexpected command' error as a granted pre-vote (raft.go:2084-2090), which is intentional for mixed versions but was not analysed for a genuinely unreachable peer.

after.meaning: The server's persisted current term and, for that term, the single candidate it has voted for (possibly itself).
after.validity_context: A term value is authoritative once persisted by setCurrentTerm; a stored vote is only consulted for the term it was cast (lastVoteTerm == req.Term).
after.durability: Written through StableStore before being used; persistence failure for the term panics, for a vote the request is rejected.
after.recovery: Read at NewRaft time into currentTerm and reused by the duplicate-requestVote check.

after.meaning: The cluster configuration currently in effect (latest) and the configuration known to be committed, each with its log index.
after.validity_context: latest is in effect from the moment its log entry is appended; committed is the newest configuration whose entry has been committed. At most one uncommitted configuration exists at a time.
after.durability: Persisted as log entries and in snapshot metadata.
after.recovery: Rebuilt at startup by restoring the snapshot and replaying configuration log entries.

after.meaning: The leader's commitIndex: the highest index the leader holds to be committed because a quorum of voters store a matching log.
after.validity_context: Only meaningful for the term in which the leader is elected; advancing it requires the quorum match to be at least startIndex (the first entry of the leader's own term).
after.durability: Not durable on the leader; recomputed from match indexes; followers persist the same entries the leader has and learn the index from LeaderCommitIndex.
after.recovery: Recomputed from replication after an election; no persisted commit index is trusted on restart.

after.meaning: Per-server record that a server's durable log agrees with the leader through at least a given index.
after.validity_context: Derived from a successful local write or a successful AppendEntries reply (last entry index), and only tracked for voters of the configuration currently installed in the commitment struct.
after.durability: In-memory only.
after.recovery: Re-derived after a leader election as replication catches up.

selections.rationale: First Candidate, grounded on the accepted map. Reading the previously unmapped FSM/apply path (fsm.go) surfaced a sourced discrepancy: ConfigurationStore documents that StoreConfiguration is invoked once a configuration log entry is committed (configuration.go:38-52), but the only call site is inside applySingle, and runFSM calls applySingle only when the FSM does NOT implement BatchingFSM (fsm.go:127-186). Separately, BatchingFSM.ApplyBatch documents that LogConfiguration entries 'will be sent' to the batching FSM (fsm.go:51-69). A FSM that implements both interfaces therefore never receives StoreConfiguration, and the configuration fact is established for it only by whatever its own ApplyBatch chooses to do. The library's own test helper (testing_batch.go:13-33) implements ApplyBatch under the batchtest build flag and simply returns nil for non-LogCommand entries, which is consistent with the discrepancy rather than with the ConfigurationStore contract. This product therefore fixes the responsibility, the attribution and a bounded discriminator; construction of the formal check is deferred to the next turn. The map is extended with the behavior and fact that support this question (b-fsm-apply-committed, f-fsm-configuration-state); no previously accepted object is modified or removed.

Investigated as Candidate claim-config-store-delivery.

selections.rationale: Construction-guided execution for the accepted unit unit-claim-config-store-delivery. Source reading says the only StoreConfiguration call site is inside applySingle (fsm.go:118), and runFSM reaches applySingle only when the FSM does not implement BatchingFSM (fsm.go:127-186), while BatchingFSM.ApplyBatch is documented to receive LogConfiguration entries (fsm.go:51-69). This exploration runs a single-voter cluster whose FSM implements BatchingFSM and ConfigurationStore, commits one LogConfiguration entry (AddNonvoter), waits for a barrier queued after it so the FSM goroutine has processed it, and reports whether StoreConfiguration was called versus whether the entry only reached ApplyBatch. Exploration output is construction knowledge only: it is not a fixed check, not Evidence and not a verdict on the obligation.

Fixed direct check for unit-claim-config-store-delivery, executing the premise that exploration already observed. Source reading (configuration.go:44-52, fsm.go:118 as the sole StoreConfiguration call site, fsm.go:127-186 as the batching bypass, testing_batch.go:13-33) predicts StoreConfiguration is unreachable for an FSM implementing BatchingFSM, while BatchingFSM.ApplyBatch documents that LogConfiguration entries are sent to batching FSMs. The clean-copy exploration of this exact scenario (operation bcaa06c272bf4890bff151ccfd995409, check a55fcacbd6224839904320183312312e) reported committed config index 4, applybatch_config_indices [1,4] and store_configuration_calls 0 with entry_delivered_to_fsm true. This product now fixes that scenario as a formal artifact: a prerequisite that the FSM implements both interfaces and that a configuration entry committed, an applicability condition that the entry was actually delivered to the FSM, and an assertion that ConfigurationStore.StoreConfiguration was invoked. The harness is unchanged from the explored bytes, so the executed premise is preserved; the obligation, oracle, identity (op_id) and scope are not weakened. The oracle is not tests_passed: the assertion is evaluated from the emitted delivery event, and the test is expected to exit 0 whether or not StoreConfiguration is called.

Checker-correspondence and applicability review of direct check 3052d8d8 (unit-claim-config-store-delivery), resolving the two open applicability issues that record the same input conflict. The observation under review is the completed execution 41bb5656bcc7426dab29aae5e648536f of the fixed bytes: scenario declared fsm_implements_batching=true and fsm_implements_configuration_store=true; the AddNonvoter configuration entry committed at index 4; ApplyBatch received indices [1,4]; store_configuration_calls was 0 and store_configuration_called false, with entry_delivered_to_fsm true. Both issues are answered by attributing each written statement to its owner and by fixing which written obligation the check encodes, not by weakening the predicate or removing the conflict.

F4 repair of an unreached experiment prerequisite. The first fixed check (3052d8d823d14854a617fe006f2a30a5) executed and its correspondence review passed, but the property comparison never completed: the assessment reported comparison_observed false with the diagnostic 'Ambiguous prerequisite association; missing scenario.op_id' and 'Admitted operation has no complete applicable result observation'. The cause is in the harness event stream, not in the obligation: the declared prerequisite alias scenario (event scenario_declared) carried the interface-implementation declarations but no op_id, while the property's identity_fields is op_id, so the correlation for the delivered result event could not associate that prerequisite. This revision changes only the harness source: the scenario_declared event now also carries op_id="cfg-1", the same identity already used by the admitted config_change_committed event and by the fsm_config_delivery result event. The plan is byte-identical (same claim, binding, prerequisites, admission_alias cfg-committed, applicability condition entry_delivered_to_fsm, assertion store_configuration_called eq true and identity op_id), so the requirement, oracle, identity, scope and legality are preserved and no property is weakened. Fresh execution of the revised bytes and a new checker-correspondence review for the resulting version are still required.

Review of revised direct check d37a13c5 (version 2 of the unit-claim-config-store-delivery artifact), whose fresh execution a898e05630e6440d97b856d7527274bd completed the previously unreached comparison. The fixed bytes emitted scenario_declared (fsm_implements_batching true, fsm_implements_configuration_store true, op_id cfg-1), config_change_committed (op_id cfg-1, config_index 4, committed true) and fsm_config_delivery (applybatch_config_indices [1,4], entry_delivered_to_fsm true, store_configuration_calls 0, store_configuration_called false). Prerequisites matched (aliases scenario and cfg-committed), the correlation for the result event matched, comparison_complete and witness_complete are true with witness index 2, and the property outcome is violated. This review supplies the required checker_correspondence item and resolves the single open applicability issue recorded on this version.

Research handoff recording the first confirmed violation on the accepted map (spec version 2) and narrowing the obsolete unknown. The confirmed execution a898e056 of the fixed check d37a13c5 observed that a FSM implementing both BatchingFSM and ConfigurationStore never receives StoreConfiguration for a committed LogConfiguration entry, while the entry is delivered through ApplyBatch. The draft map is updated only where the answered unknown lived: the batching branch of b-fsm-apply-committed now carries the observed conditional relationship, and the unknowns of that behavior and of f-fsm-configuration-state are narrowed to the unresolved support/contract question. No meaning, edge, identity or observation scope is changed, so the existing obligations and results stay on their original basis; a different, still-unresolved core A1/A2 discriminator will be selected next rather than extending this one into variants.

feedback.answered: For a FSM implementing both BatchingFSM and ConfigurationStore, the library does not invoke ConfigurationStore.StoreConfiguration for a committed LogConfiguration entry. The revised direct check d37a13c5 executed its fixed bytes (execution a898e056): prerequisites matched, comparison_complete and witness_complete are true, and the property c-store-config-called evaluated false because store_configuration_calls stayed 0 while the configuration entry reached the FSM through ApplyBatch (indices [1,4]) and the admitted entry committed at index 4 with entry_delivered_to_fsm true. The obligation claim-config-store-delivery is therefore confirmed violated in the checked scope; the earlier blocker (an uncorrelated prerequisite because the scenario declaration lacked the op_id identity) was a harness observation-encoding defect and was repaired by an F4 revision that changed only the harness source.
remaining: Whether a FSM implementing both BatchingFSM and ConfigurationStore is a supported configuration, or whether ConfigurationStore is intended only for non-batching FSMs, is unresolved; under the latter reading the correct disposition would be a contract/documentation clarification rather than a delivery defect.
The confirmed observation covers one committed configuration entry delivered to one batching FSM on a single-voter carrier; multi-voter commitment paths and other log types are not characterised.

No core A1/A2 question has been selected yet; the accepted overview and the remaining unread surfaces (net/tcp transport framing, inmem transport heartbeat fast path, observer plumbing, config reload) still hold unexplored discriminators.
feedback.rationale: The map update records the transition from hypothesis to observed behaviour for the batching FSM configuration-delivery path, and narrows the residual unknown to the contract question that the check deliberately did not decide. This is the natural handoff from the first confirmed obligation: the requirement, the confirmed observation and its scope limitation stay in their own records, while the overview keeps the core picture unchanged.

b-fsm-apply-committed.rationale: The answered half of this behavior's unknown is replaced by the now-observed conditional relationship, without changing its meaning, triggers, producers/consumers or observation scope: for a FSM implementing both BatchingFSM and ConfigurationStore, a committed LogConfiguration entry is delivered only through ApplyBatch and StoreConfiguration is not invoked. selections.rationale: Fixed direct check for unit-claim-timeout-now-attribution (obligation claim-timeout-now-attribution). The harness declares a TimeoutNow sender that is not a voter of the receiver's bootstrapped two-voter configuration and drives the production dispatch seam processRPC, then measures whether the receiver abandoned its known leader, entered candidate state and raised the transfer privilege. The property is an implication: if the sender is not a configured voter, the privilege must not be granted; the declarative prerequisite fixes that sender scope independently of the result, and identity is the declared op_id. Two controls bracket the comparison: a configured-voter sender (shows the handler is otherwise reachable) and an out-of-window sender (shows the version window is the only guard). Local construction testing in a copy of the captured module already shows the asymmetry - the unattributed sender was honoured (leader node2 -> cleared, Follower -> Candidate, privilege false -> true) exactly like the configured sender, while the out-of-window request was rejected with 'operation not supported with current protocol version' and changed nothing - but that run is construction knowledge only; this product fixes the bytes, premises and oracle for fresh controller execution. Nodes are built with skipStartup and the sender identifier is fabricated, which is disclosed as a limitation: the check establishes the handler's decision for a sender absent from the receiver's configuration, not that a removed running node reaches it.

feedback.answered: A suspected defect was investigated and explained rather than escalated. A node whose log is empty but which holds a newer snapshot - the state RecoverCluster deliberately produces by truncating the whole log, and also reachable with TrailingLogs=0 when the FSM has applied through the snapshot index - looked as if it would restart at log index 0, reuse indices below the snapshot and leave committed client entries unapplied and unanswered. It does not: getLastIndex returns max(lastLogIndex, lastSnapshotIndex) and getLastEntry returns the snapshot's index/term when the snapshot is newer (state.go:157-174), while NewRaft reads the log's last index and restoreSnapshot sets lastApplied and the last snapshot (api.go:631-664). The node therefore advertises and resumes at the snapshot index, and dispatchLogs starts from getLastIndex()+1. The map gains the mechanism as behavior b-stable-position-reconstruction and fact f-stable-log-position so the false lead is closed with sources instead of being re-investigated.
remaining: ReloadConfig notification scope remains a low-consequence lead: only a decreased HeartbeatTimeout signals the notify channels, so a decreased LeaderLeaseTimeout is not picked up until the current lease timer fires (api.go:713-741, config.go:260-290).

The three confirmed findings each keep an open premise: real-deployment reachability for the unconfigured TimeoutNow sender, the election consequence of the heartbeat fast path, and whether batching FSMs are contractually exempt from ConfigurationStore.

feedback.answered: New sourced lead on the snapshot receive path, prompted by the log/snapshot position mechanism just recorded. installSnapshot ends by setting lastApplied and lastSnapshot and then either removing all old logs (monotonic stores) or compacting only up to the installed snapshot index (raft.go:1928-1953), and it never calls setLastLog - the only callers of setLastLog are NewRaft, liveBootstrap, restoreUserSnapshot, dispatchLogs and appendEntries. Its compaction keeps entries above the snapshot index (snapshot.go:213-259 uses maxLog = min(snapIdx, lastLogIdx-trailing)), so a follower that already holds a longer divergent branch retains that tail, and getLastEntry continues to report the tail's index/term even though the FSM state and the committed/latest configuration now come from the installed snapshot.
remaining: Whether a follower whose log is longer than the installed snapshot is reachable: the leader sends a snapshot when its own log no longer covers the follower's nextIndex, and a follower with a longer divergent branch can be driven to that state, but the exact sequence was not established.

after.reason: Sourced asymmetry found while reading the snapshot receive path: after a successful InstallSnapshot the handler updates lastApplied and lastSnapshot and then compacts (raft.go:1928-1953), but it never calls setLastLog, and its only setLastLog callers are NewRaft, liveBootstrap, restoreUserSnapshot, dispatchLogs and appendEntries. Its compaction removes entries only up to the installed snapshot index (snapshot.go:213-259, maxLog = min(snapIdx, lastLogIdx-trailing)), so any entries the follower already holds beyond that index survive. before.reason: Sourced asymmetry found while reading the snapshot receive path: after a successful InstallSnapshot the handler updates lastApplied and lastSnapshot and then compacts (raft.go:1928-1953), but it never calls setLastLog, and its only setLastLog callers are NewRaft, liveBootstrap, restoreUserSnapshot, dispatchLogs and appendEntries. Its compaction removes entries only up to the installed snapshot index (snapshot.go:213-259, maxLog = min(snapIdx, lastLogIdx-trailing)), so any entries the follower already holds beyond that index survive. For a follower whose log is longer than the installed snapshot (a divergent branch), getLastEntry therefore keeps returning that tail's index/term until the next matching AppendEntries truncates it, even though the FSM state and committed configuration now come from the snapshot. Whether such a longer divergent branch is reachable and whether the window has a consequence (vote comparisons use getLastEntry) is not established.

feedback.answered: Two further entry-path suspicions were checked against source and closed rather than escalated. (1) The protocol-version gate looks as if it could underflow at the minimum: checkRPCHeader rejects when header.ProtocolVersion < r.config().ProtocolVersion-1 (raft.go:60-70), so a node configured at ProtocolVersionMin could in principle reject every peer. It cannot, because ProtocolVersion is a signed int rather than an unsigned type (config.go:99 with Min 0 and Max 3), so the expression evaluates to -1 at the minimum and no valid header is rejected. This also fixes the reading of the heartbeat finding: the gate that the fast path skips is a real, bounded window (-1 .. Max), not an accidentally impossible one. (2) liveBootstrap looked as though it could bootstrap a node that already has state, because it forces the current term to 1 and sets the last log from the bootstrap entry; it cannot, because BootstrapCluster refuses when HasExistingState reports state (api.go:252-259), and liveBootstrap is only reachable through the bootstrap channel on a node that has not been bootstrapped.

formation.explanation: A follower whose heartbeat timer expires while it is an eligible voter transitions to Candidate and runCandidate starts a pre-vote campaign (preElectSelf) that proposes currentTerm+1 without touching the term. Each other voter answers in requestPreVote with the leader-stickiness, membership and log-up-to-date guards and without persisting anything. If a quorum of pre-votes is granted the candidate runs electSelf, which persists the new term and a self-vote, then requests votes; voters persist the vote in requestVote subject to the same guards plus one-vote-per-term. The first tally to reach quorumSize() sets the candidate to Leader. The leader then appends a no-op for its term and replicates; the commitment struct advances commitIndex only when an actual quorum's matchIndex reaches at least startIndex, the first index of the leader's own term.

context.explanation: Authority is the durable current term plus the durable per-term vote; there is no global leader identity. setCurrentTerm persists a term before it is exposed and setState clears the known leader on every transition. A newer term seen in RequestVote or AppendEntries forces a step-down and term update, so context is lost by observation, not by a clock. Leadership transfer pre-replicates to the target and sends TimeoutNow; the target marks candidateFromLeadershipTransfer so that it skips pre-vote and is not stepped down by an equal-term AppendEntries from the outgoing leader, and the flag is cleared after the candidate run. The configuration context is the pair (latest, committed); latest is in effect from the moment its entry is appended.

connection.explanation: The two lines meet in three places. (1) Eligibility for formation is read from the configuration context: only voters of the latest configuration are asked for votes and only their match indexes count for commitment, and the commitment struct is rebuilt from the configuration at leader setup and at each configuration change. (2) The leader's advancement duty is gated by its term context: configurationChangeChIfStable is only non-nil once latest==committed and the leader has committed an entry of its own term (commitIndex >= startIndex), which is why a no-op is dispatched on election even with no client work. (3) Old work is bounded by present authority: a persisted vote is only honoured for its own term, an AppendEntries reply that reports a newer term drives handleStaleTerm and a step-down, a conflicting suffix truncation rolls latest back to committed, and on step-down the leader fails all inflight log futures with ErrLeadershipLost while replication goroutines are stopped.

open_details: appendEntries has an explicit TODO (raft.go:1541): if StoreLogs fails after a truncation, lastLog is left stale. Whether any real store can fail there, and its consequence, is unresolved.
electSelf returns a nil response channel when persisting the self-vote fails (raft.go:2023), leaving the candidate to wait out its election timer; this is a storage-failure path only.

checkLeaderLease assumes leaderState.replState contains every voter of the latest configuration (raft.go:1054); ordering on the main thread appears to guarantee this, but a nil-map lookup would panic and was not tested.

The pre-vote path treats a transport 'unexpected command' error as a granted pre-vote (raft.go:2084-2090), which is intentional for mixed versions but was not analysed for a genuinely unreachable peer.

selections.rationale: Independent second scenario for the already-accepted requirement unit-claim-timeout-now-attribution, kept with the same obligation rather than split into a new question. The first check established that TimeoutNow hands the transfer privilege to a sender outside the receiver's configuration; this one measures the consequence the finding's importance rests on, at the voter that must honour the resulting vote request: with the privilege set, a voter that already follows a different leader grants the vote to a configured candidate, while the identical request without the flag is rejected and the flag does not defeat the configuration-membership check. Identity is the declared op_id; the oracle reads the emitted grant decision, not tests_passed. Local construction testing in a copy of the captured module already produced that pattern (granted true, granted false, granted false), but that run is construction knowledge only; this product fixes the bytes, premises and oracle for fresh controller execution. Nodes are built with skipStartup and the vote is driven through the production dispatch processRPC, with the known leader set through the same accessors appendEntries uses; no target code is modified.

Review of the second-scenario direct check 38aa8959 (unit-claim-timeout-now-attribution), whose fresh execution ec71e08710e746bbbe6e7268f032377e completed the comparison with the declarative prerequisite matched, comparison_complete and witness_complete true, and the assertion holding: with the transfer privilege set a voter that already followed node2 granted a vote to the configured candidate node3 (granted true), while the identical request without the flag was rejected (granted false) and the flag did not defeat the membership check (unconfigured candidate, granted false). The result is a corroboration of the privilege's mechanism, not a new violation: the first scenario of the same requirement already carries the violated comparison. This review supplies the required checker_correspondence item and re-resolves the claim-level applicability issue, which is open again for this artifact because the earlier resolution answers its own artifact lineage.

Second scenario for the already-accepted requirement unit-claim-heartbeat-header-gate, kept with the same obligation. The first scenario fixed that the fast path acts on an out-of-window pure heartbeat the normal path rejects; this one measures the downstream consequence on the formation path: after that heartbeat the receiver reports the foreign sender as its known leader, and an otherwise acceptable vote request from a configured candidate is then rejected, while the same request on a node that never saw the heartbeat is granted. Identity is the declared op_id; the oracle reads the receiver's leader state and the grant decision from the emitted events, not tests_passed. Local construction testing in a copy of the captured module already produced that pattern (ghost_leader_adopted true with legitimate_vote_granted false, versus false and true on the control), but that run is construction knowledge only; this product fixes the bytes, premises and oracle for fresh controller execution. The heartbeat is delivered through processHeartbeat, the body of the handler installed by SetHeartbeatHandler, because net_transport's fast path is TCP-only and network access is disabled; the classification is a sourced premise and no target code is modified.

Review of the second-scenario direct check f8caf123 (unit-claim-heartbeat-header-gate), whose fresh execution 7628b537f51c4a868e8ebb80cf019fc2 completed the comparison with the declarative prerequisite matched, comparison_complete and witness_complete true, and the implication holding: after an out-of-window pure heartbeat the receiver adopted the sender as its known leader (ghost_leader_adopted true, known_leader_id ghost) and rejected an otherwise acceptable vote request from the configured candidate node2 (legitimate_vote_granted false), while the same request on a node that never saw the heartbeat was granted (true). The result corroborates the consequence of the skipped guard rather than adding a violation; the first scenario of the same requirement already carries the violated comparison. feedback.answered: Both confirmed findings whose importance rested on an unmeasured consequence now carry measured consequence evidence, recorded on the behaviors that own the mechanisms. For the heartbeat fast path (second scenario f8caf123, execution 7628b537): after an out-of-window heartbeat the receiver adopted the sender as its known leader and rejected an otherwise acceptable vote from a configured candidate, while a node that never saw the heartbeat granted it - so the skipped gate suppresses a legitimate election, not only a guard comparison. feedback.answered: A further sourced discrepancy was found in the transport configuration surface and recorded as a lead rather than escalated. NetworkTransportConfig documents that 'For InstallSnapshot, we multiply the timeout by (SnapshotSize / TimeoutScale)' (net_transport.go:161-163), but that struct has no TimeoutScale field: the field lives only on the transport itself (net_transport.go:109-110), and NewNetworkTransportWithConfig unconditionally writes DefaultTimeoutScale into it (net_transport.go:226-238), ignoring anything a caller might have expected to configure. So the documented knob for scaling the snapshot send deadline is inert through the public configuration struct, and the only way to change it is to mutate the exported transport field after construction, which the snapshot sender in InstallSnapshot reads directly. items.rationale: Requirement versus encoded predicate: S34 documents ConfigurationStore and states that StoreConfiguration is invoked once a log entry containing a configuration change is committed; property c-store-config-called asserts exactly that (store_configuration_called eq true) for the FSM that declares ConfigurationStore. Entry and caller duties: the harness elects a leader, re-establishes an own-term committed entry with a Barrier so configurationChangeChIfStable is open, then drives AddNonvoter on a single-voter cluster where the LogConfiguration entry commits under the existing configuration because nonvoters are excluded from the commitment quorum; no caller duty of the checked premise is skipped. Oracle: the property is evaluated from the emitted fsm_config_delivery event fields (S39 applySingle path is the obligation's implementation site, S36/S37 locate delivery), not from tests_passed, so a process that exits 0 while store_configuration_called stays false is still a violated comparison. Identity: op_id cfg-1 is carried by both the committed prerequisite event and the delivery event. Observation path and completion: the Barrier queued after the configuration entry means the single FIFO fsmMutateCh has been drained through that entry (and index 4 is separately visible in applybatch_config_indices) before the sample is taken; both futures returned nil and the run completed with exit 0. findings.description: Confirmed violation of: For every FSM that implements ConfigurationStore, the library must invoke StoreConfiguration(index, configuration) for each committed configuration log entry that it delivers to the FSM, so that a persistent FSM can reconstruct configuration without an external snapshot.

Confirmed violation of: Every AppendEntries RPC a server processes, including a pure heartbeat handled by the transport fast path, is subject to the same RPC-header compatibility check that the normal RPC path applies before appendEntries, so a peer outside the supported protocol-version window cannot step the server down, advance its persisted term, be adopted as the known leader or refresh its last contact.

Confirmed violation of: A TimeoutNow request is honoured only when its sender is attributed to the receiver's authority context, at minimum a voter of the receiver's latest configuration, so that a peer outside that configuration cannot clear the receiver's known leader, force it into candidate state and hand it the transfer privilege that skips pre-vote and makes other voters grant votes despite having a leader.

Confirmed violation of: On a successful InstallSnapshot at index N, a receiver that no longer holds a log entry at N matching the snapshot's last included term must discard the log entries above N, so that its effective last entry and its later vote comparisons and replication decisions are not based on a branch the snapshot did not confirm.

Confirmed violation of: On a successful InstallSnapshot at index N, a receiver that no longer holds a log entry at N matching the snapshot's last included term must discard the log entries above N, so that its effective last entry and its later vote comparisons and replication decisions are not based on a branch the snapshot did not confirm.

scope.description: A single Raft node whose FSM implements ConfigurationStore, processing a committed LogConfiguration entry. The obligation concerns delivery of the configuration entry to the FSM, not the correctness of the configuration value itself.

units.rationale: First Candidate, grounded on the accepted map. Reading the previously unmapped FSM/apply path (fsm.go) surfaced a sourced discrepancy: ConfigurationStore documents that StoreConfiguration is invoked once a configuration log entry is committed (configuration.go:38-52), but the only call site is inside applySingle, and runFSM calls applySingle only when the FSM does NOT implement BatchingFSM (fsm.go:127-186). Separately, BatchingFSM.ApplyBatch documents that LogConfiguration entries 'will be sent' to the batching FSM (fsm.go:51-69). A FSM that implements both interfaces therefore never receives StoreConfiguration, and the configuration fact is established for it only by whatever its own ApplyBatch chooses to do. The library's own test helper (testing_batch.go:13-33) implements ApplyBatch under the batchtest build flag and simply returns nil for non-LogCommand entries, which is consistent with the discrepancy rather than with the ConfigurationStore contract. This product therefore fixes the responsibility, the attribution and a bounded discriminator; construction of the formal check is deferred to the next turn. The map is extended with the behavior and fact that support this question (b-fsm-apply-committed, f-fsm-configuration-state); no previously accepted object is modified or removed.

audit_question.question: When a FSM implements both BatchingFSM and ConfigurationStore, does the library invoke StoreConfiguration(index, configuration) for a committed LogConfiguration entry, as the ConfigurationStore contract states, or does the batching dispatch in runFSM make that invocation unreachable?
audit_question.importance: ConfigurationStore exists so a persistent FSM can treat its own state as a complete snapshot and recover without an external snapshot (configuration.go:44-52). If the invocation is unreachable for batching FSMs, an application that implements both interfaces silently loses the only library-provided delivery of committed configuration changes, which matters for recovery and for the FSM's own view of cluster membership. This is an implementation/contract gap, not a consensus-safety violation; it is classified implementation_semantics.

BatchingFSM.ApplyBatch's own doc says LogConfiguration entries will be sent to the batching FSM, which is consistent with the batching FSM being expected to persist configuration itself; this may mean ConfigurationStore is intended to be a non-batching-only interface and the interface comment is merely imprecise.

audit_question.question: Does the heartbeat fast path apply the RPC-header compatibility gate that the normal AppendEntries path applies, so that a peer whose RPCHeader.ProtocolVersion is outside the window checkRPCHeader accepts cannot step this server down, advance its persisted term, be adopted as known leader and refresh its last contact?
audit_question.importance: The header gate is the only guard that keeps a server from participating with a peer outside its supported protocol-version window. On the fast path a pure heartbeat still reaches appendEntries, which can persist a newer term, transition the receiver out of candidate/leader state, record the sender as the known leader and refresh lastContact. If an out-of-window peer can reach that path, this server can be held out of its own elections by a peer whose RPCs the same process rejects on every other route, which is an availability consequence on a core formation path; the guard asymmetry itself is an implementation-semantics concern.

audit_question.question: Is a TimeoutNow request honoured only when its sender is attributed to the receiver's authority context - a voter of the receiver's latest configuration - or can any peer whose RPC header passes the version window make the receiver clear its known leader, enter candidate state and receive the transfer privilege that skips pre-vote and makes peers vote despite having a leader?

The receive handler (S49) checks nothing: the request carries only an RPCHeader with no term (S48), and the handler clears the leader, sets Candidate and raises the privilege before a single validation. The vote RPCs by contrast reject a candidate that is not in the configuration and are granted despite a leader only when that privilege is set (S6, S21). If a node that is not a member of the receiver's configuration can reach this handler - a removed server or a stale node still running the same protocol version - it can force term inflation and an election that peers will vote for, which is an authority-transition defect on a core path.

audit_question.question: After a successful InstallSnapshot at index N, does the receiver discard the log entries it cannot reconcile with the snapshot - so that its effective last entry never comes from a branch the snapshot did not confirm - or does it retain and report a tail above N even when it no longer holds an entry at N matching the snapshot's term?
audit_question.importance: The receiver's last log entry is what it advertises in RequestVote and what it uses for its own vote comparisons, and the AppendEntries success rule is what lets a leader count it towards a quorum. If a receiver installs a snapshot at N while keeping entries above N that the snapshot's history did not confirm, then until the next matching AppendEntries arrives the node votes and is counted on a log position that no longer describes its state; a candidate elected on that position would have to be brought back by a snapshot. The Raft snapshot protocol requires discarding the log in exactly this case, so the duty is well grounded rather than a stylistic preference.

selections.rationale: Invalid submitted input path

First, partial-but-usable core map for the hashicorp/raft snapshot (module github.com/hashicorp/raft, commit c0dc6a0b). The submission records the two core relationships required by the activity roles and, crucially, their connection, from read code plus the membership design document: (A1) qualified support for decision formation and legal advancement, realized as pre-vote campaign -> real vote campaign -> per-term vote grants -> leader no-op + replication -> quorum commitment at or above the first index of the leader's term; and (A2) context validity and acquisition/transfer/loss of authority, realized as the durable current term plus per-term vote, step-down-and-bump on newer terms, and leadership transfer via TimeoutNow with the candidateFromLeadershipTransfer exemption. The connection is sourced: formation eligibility and the commitment quorum are read from the latest configuration; configuration changes are only opened once latest==committed and the leader has committed an entry of its own term (configurationChangeChIfStable), which is why a no-op is always dispatched on election; and old work is bounded by present authority (votes honoured only for their own term, an AppendEntries reply reporting a newer term driving handleStaleTerm/step-down, conflicting-suffix truncation rolling latest back to committed, and inflight futures failed with ErrLeadershipLost on step-down). Residual local anomalies are recorded under core_overview.open_details rather than blocking the overview: the appendEntries StoreLogs-failure TODO leaving lastLog stale (raft.go:1541), electSelf returning a nil response channel on self-vote persistence failure (raft.go:2023), and checkLeaderLease assuming a replState entry exists for every latest-config voter (raft.go:1054). Several high-consequence paths remain explicitly unmapped surfaces (installSnapshot body, leader-side snapshot shipping, runFSM, snapshot lifecycle), and the next step is to read them and pick a sourced discriminator rather than to treat this map as coverage. No obligation or check is claimed here.

after.purpose: Qualified support for decision formation and legal advancement: elect a leader and extend/commit the replicated log.
after.realization_summary: A candidate runs a pre-vote campaign (preElectSelf) that does not change its term and, on winning it, a real campaign (electSelf) that increments and persists the term and asks voters for a vote. Followers decide the vote in requestVote/requestPreVote with leader-stickiness, log up-to-date and one-vote-per-term guards. The elected leader dispatches a no-op for its term, replicates to each peer (followerReplication), and advances the commit index through the commitment struct once a quorum's matchIndex reaches at least the first entry of the leader's own term.

formation.explanation: A follower whose heartbeat timer expires while it is an eligible voter transitions to Candidate and runCandidate starts a pre-vote campaign (preElectSelf) that proposes currentTerm+1 without touching the term. Each other voter answers in requestPreVote with the leader-stickiness, membership and log-up-to-date guards and without persisting anything. If a quorum of pre-votes is granted the candidate runs electSelf, which persists the new term and a self-vote, then requests votes; voters persist the vote in requestVote subject to the same guards plus one-vote-per-term. The first tally to reach quorumSize() sets the candidate to Leader. The leader then appends a no-op for its term and replicates; the commitment struct advances commitIndex only when an actual quorum's matchIndex reaches at least startIndex, the first index of the leader's own term.

context.explanation: Authority is the durable current term plus the durable per-term vote; there is no global leader identity. setCurrentTerm persists a term before it is exposed and setState clears the known leader on every transition. A newer term seen in RequestVote or AppendEntries forces a step-down and term update, so context is lost by observation, not by a clock. Leadership transfer pre-replicates to the target and sends TimeoutNow; the target marks candidateFromLeadershipTransfer so that it skips pre-vote and is not stepped down by an equal-term AppendEntries from the outgoing leader, and the flag is cleared after the candidate run. The configuration context is the pair (latest, committed); latest is in effect from the moment its entry is appended.

connection.explanation: The two lines meet in three places. (1) Eligibility for formation is read from the configuration context: only voters of the latest configuration are asked for votes and only their match indexes count for commitment, and the commitment struct is rebuilt from the configuration at leader setup and at each configuration change. (2) The leader's advancement duty is gated by its term context: configurationChangeChIfStable is only non-nil once latest==committed and the leader has committed an entry of its own term (commitIndex >= startIndex), which is why a no-op is dispatched on election even with no client work. (3) Old work is bounded by present authority: a persisted vote is only honoured for its own term, an AppendEntries reply that reports a newer term drives handleStaleTerm and a step-down, a conflicting suffix truncation rolls latest back to committed, and on step-down the leader fails all inflight log futures with ErrLeadershipLost while replication goroutines are stopped.

open_details: appendEntries has an explicit TODO (raft.go:1541): if StoreLogs fails after a truncation, lastLog is left stale. Whether any real store can fail there, and its consequence, is unresolved.

checkLeaderLease assumes leaderState.replState contains every voter of the latest configuration (raft.go:1054); ordering on the main thread appears to guarantee this, but a nil-map lookup would panic and was not tested.

The pre-vote path treats a transport 'unexpected command' error as a granted pre-vote (raft.go:2084-2090), which is intentional for mixed versions but was not analysed for a genuinely unreachable peer.

selections.rationale: First Candidate, grounded on the accepted map. Reading the previously unmapped FSM/apply path (fsm.go) surfaced a sourced discrepancy: ConfigurationStore documents that StoreConfiguration is invoked once a configuration log entry is committed (configuration.go:38-52), but the only call site is inside applySingle, and runFSM calls applySingle only when the FSM does NOT implement BatchingFSM (fsm.go:127-186). Separately, BatchingFSM.ApplyBatch documents that LogConfiguration entries 'will be sent' to the batching FSM (fsm.go:51-69). A FSM that implements both interfaces therefore never receives StoreConfiguration, and the configuration fact is established for it only by whatever its own ApplyBatch chooses to do. The library's own test helper (testing_batch.go:13-33) implements ApplyBatch under the batchtest build flag and simply returns nil for non-LogCommand entries, which is consistent with the discrepancy rather than with the ConfigurationStore contract. This product therefore fixes the responsibility, the attribution and a bounded discriminator; construction of the formal check is deferred to the next turn. The map is extended with the behavior and fact that support this question (b-fsm-apply-committed, f-fsm-configuration-state); no previously accepted object is modified or removed.

Source reading says the only StoreConfiguration call site is inside applySingle (fsm.go:118), and runFSM reaches applySingle only when the FSM does not implement BatchingFSM (fsm.go:127-186), while BatchingFSM.ApplyBatch is documented to receive LogConfiguration entries (fsm.go:51-69). Fixed direct check for unit-claim-config-store-delivery, executing the premise that exploration already observed. Source reading (configuration.go:44-52, fsm.go:118 as the sole StoreConfiguration call site, fsm.go:127-186 as the batching bypass, testing_batch.go:13-33) predicts StoreConfiguration is unreachable for an FSM implementing BatchingFSM, while BatchingFSM.ApplyBatch documents that LogConfiguration entries are sent to batching FSMs. The clean-copy exploration of this exact scenario (operation bcaa06c272bf4890bff151ccfd995409, check a55fcacbd6224839904320183312312e) reported committed config index 4, applybatch_config_indices [1,4] and store_configuration_calls 0 with entry_delivered_to_fsm true. The harness is unchanged from the explored bytes, so the executed premise is preserved; the obligation, oracle, identity (op_id) and scope are not weakened. The oracle is not tests_passed: the assertion is evaluated from the emitted delivery event, and the test is expected to exit 0 whether or not StoreConfiguration is called.

Reading the previously deferred transport surfaces exposed that processHeartbeat is the only entry into appendEntries that skips checkRPCHeader, and that the network transport routes pure heartbeats to it. feedback.answered: New sourced lead on a core path, not an obligation: the appendEntries handler has two entry paths with different guards. raft.go:1390-1413 routes normal RPCs through checkRPCHeader (which enforces the supported protocol-version window) before dispatching AppendEntries, while raft.go:1415-1436 (processHeartbeat, installed as the transport fast path at api.go:616) calls appendEntries directly. net_transport.go:660-686 classifies a pure AppendEntries with Term != 0, a leader address, no entries, PrevLogEntry/PrevLogTerm zero and LeaderCommitIndex zero as a heartbeat and net_transport.go:724-733 hands it to the handler without any header check. On that path appendEntries can still step a receiver down and persist a newer term, adopt the sender as known leader and refresh lastContact.
remaining: Whether a peer whose RPCHeader.ProtocolVersion falls outside the window checkRPCHeader rejects can reach a pure heartbeat to a follower in practice, and whether any consequence follows beyond the version gate itself.

Whether the omission is deliberate (the fast path being understood as a shortcut that assumes already-validated peers) or an unintended asymmetry: no comment on processHeartbeat or on the transport fast path states that the header gate is intentionally skipped.
The confirmed ConfigurationStore delivery violation is settled in scope and needs no further work; the open question there (whether batching FSMs are contractually exempt) stays a limitation.
feedback.rationale: The new Surface preserves a real, sourced asymmetry between two entry paths for the same request type without presuming it is a defect. The next step is premise investigation: read checkRPCHeader's callers and the transport's version handling to decide whether an attributed obligation is available or whether the asymmetry is intentional design.
