It records that the same AppendEntriesRequest shape is subject to two different entry paths: processRPC applies checkRPCHeader before appendEntries, while the heartbeat fast path processHeartbeat reaches appendEntries with no header check, and net_transport routes pure heartbeats to that handler. after.reason: Sourced discrepancy in the appendEntries entry paths: processRPC calls checkRPCHeader before dispatching AppendEntries (raft.go:1390-1413), but the heartbeat fast path processHeartbeat calls appendEntries directly with no read of checkRPCHeader (raft.go:1415-1436), and net_transport routes any pure AppendEntries heartbeat (Term != 0, leader addr present, no entries, no prev-log fields, LeaderCommitIndex 0) to that handler (net_transport.go:660-686, 724-733). An AppendEntries whose RPCHeader.ProtocolVersion is outside the supported window that checkRPCHeader rejects on the normal path would therefore still be accepted on the fast path, where appendEntries can step the receiver down, persist a newer term, set the sender as known leader and refresh lastContact. Whether the window outside the fast path's route is reachable with a legal peer and what consequence it has is not established.

selections.rationale: Second obligation, grounded on the accepted map. before.durability: In-memory only; not persisted, so a restart loses it.
before.recovery: No recovery; a restarted node starts without the privilege.
unknowns: no obligation yet ties the granting of this privilege to the sender's authority, and the request carries no term with which to check it

after.meaning: The privilege held by a receiver of a TimeoutNow request to skip the pre-vote campaign and to send votes that peers grant even though they already have a leader.
after.validity_context: Set by timeoutNow on receipt of any TimeoutNow request that passes the RPC-header version window, and cleared after each runCandidate invocation; it is the only stated protection against reuse.
after.durability: In-memory only; not persisted, so a restart loses it.
after.recovery: No recovery; a restarted node starts without the privilege.
unknowns: The privilege is granted for any in-window TimeoutNow request, including one whose sender the receiver's configuration does not contain (observed, execution 554a0abc); whether that reachability is real and whether the design intends to trust leader discipline remain open.

Whether that delay has a consequence worth investigating was not established, and the other reloadable fields are read per iteration by their loops. Low consequence; recorded rather than escalated.

feedback.answered: A suspected defect was investigated and explained rather than escalated. A node whose log is empty but which holds a newer snapshot - the state RecoverCluster deliberately produces by truncating the whole log, and also reachable with TrailingLogs=0 when the FSM has applied through the snapshot index - looked as if it would restart at log index 0, reuse indices below the snapshot and leave committed client entries unapplied and unanswered. It does not: getLastIndex returns max(lastLogIndex, lastSnapshotIndex) and getLastEntry returns the snapshot's index/term when the snapshot is newer (state.go:157-174), while NewRaft reads the log's last index and restoreSnapshot sets lastApplied and the last snapshot (api.go:631-664). The node therefore advertises and resumes at the snapshot index, and dispatchLogs starts from getLastIndex()+1. The map gains the mechanism as behavior b-stable-position-reconstruction and fact f-stable-log-position so the false lead is closed with sources instead of being re-investigated.
remaining: ReloadConfig notification scope remains a low-consequence lead: only a decreased HeartbeatTimeout signals the notify channels, so a decreased LeaderLeaseTimeout is not picked up until the current lease timer fires (api.go:713-741, config.go:260-290).

The three confirmed findings each keep an open premise: real-deployment reachability for the unconfigured TimeoutNow sender, the election consequence of the heartbeat fast path, and whether batching FSMs are contractually exempt from ConfigurationStore.

after.meaning: The node's position in stable storage: the last log entry it holds together with the last snapshot it holds, and the effective last index/term derived from the two.

after.recovery: NewRaft reads the log's last index, restoreSnapshot sets lastApplied and the last snapshot, and restoreSnapshot does not need to rewrite lastLog because the accessors take the maximum.
unknowns: none recorded: the max-of-two accessors explain the empty-log-with-newer-snapshot case that would otherwise look like index reuse

feedback.answered: New sourced lead on the snapshot receive path, prompted by the log/snapshot position mechanism just recorded. installSnapshot ends by setting lastApplied and lastSnapshot and then either removing all old logs (monotonic stores) or compacting only up to the installed snapshot index (raft.go:1928-1953), and it never calls setLastLog - the only callers of setLastLog are NewRaft, liveBootstrap, restoreUserSnapshot, dispatchLogs and appendEntries. Its compaction keeps entries above the snapshot index (snapshot.go:213-259 uses maxLog = min(snapIdx, lastLogIdx-trailing)), so a follower that already holds a longer divergent branch retains that tail, and getLastEntry continues to report the tail's index/term even though the FSM state and the committed/latest configuration now come from the installed snapshot.
remaining: Whether a follower whose log is longer than the installed snapshot is reachable: the leader sends a snapshot when its own log no longer covers the follower's nextIndex, and a follower with a longer divergent branch can be driven to that state, but the exact sequence was not established.

Whether the window has a consequence: vote comparisons use getLastEntry, so during the window the follower's self-report and its vote decisions reflect the tail rather than the installed snapshot; the next matching AppendEntries truncates the tail and calls setLastLog.

after.reason: Sourced asymmetry found while reading the snapshot receive path: after a successful InstallSnapshot the handler updates lastApplied and lastSnapshot and then compacts (raft.go:1928-1953), but it never calls setLastLog, and its only setLastLog callers are NewRaft, liveBootstrap, restoreUserSnapshot, dispatchLogs and appendEntries. Its compaction removes entries only up to the installed snapshot index (snapshot.go:213-259, maxLog = min(snapIdx, lastLogIdx-trailing)), so any entries the follower already holds beyond that index survive. selections.rationale: Fourth candidate, grounded on the accepted map. The snapshot receive path adopts the installed snapshot's index and term but never aligns the log with it: it does not set the last log, and its compaction stops at the snapshot index, while the effective last entry is the maximum of log and snapshot position. A direct local run of the receive path (single node, log seeded to index 5, snapshot installed at index 3) produced compaction from 1 to 3, two surviving entries, lastApplied 3 and an effective last entry of (5, term 1). Identity is the declared op_id; the oracle reads emitted event fields, not tests_passed. feedback.answered: Two further entry-path suspicions were checked against source and closed rather than escalated. (1) The protocol-version gate looks as if it could underflow at the minimum: checkRPCHeader rejects when header.ProtocolVersion < r.config().ProtocolVersion-1 (raft.go:60-70), so a node configured at ProtocolVersionMin could in principle reject every peer. It cannot, because ProtocolVersion is a signed int rather than an unsigned type (config.go:99 with Min 0 and Max 3), so the expression evaluates to -1 at the minimum and no valid header is rejected. This also fixes the reading of the heartbeat finding: the gate that the fast path skips is a real, bounded window (-1 .. Max), not an accidentally impossible one. (2) liveBootstrap looked as though it could bootstrap a node that already has state, because it forces the current term to 1 and sets the last log from the bootstrap entry; it cannot, because BootstrapCluster refuses when HasExistingState reports state (api.go:252-259), and liveBootstrap is only reachable through the bootstrap channel on a node that has not been bootstrapped.
remaining: ReloadConfig notification scope remains a low-consequence lead: only a decreased HeartbeatTimeout signals the notify channels, so a decreased LeaderLeaseTimeout is not picked up until the current lease timer fires.

The processHeartbeat concurrency contract is an unresolved independent limit: its comment says main-thread only while the transport invokes it from a connection goroutine, and the fields it touches are individually protected.

feedback.answered: A third suspicion from the snapshot area was checked and closed. FileSnapshotStore.List builds its result with `for _, meta := range snapshots { snapMeta = append(snapMeta, &meta.SnapshotMeta) }` (file_snapshot.go:226-242) over the pointers returned by getSnapshots (file_snapshot.go:244-289). That pattern is the classic aliasing shape - every appended pointer would address the same range variable - and this module's go.mod declares go 1.20, which is below the version at which per-iteration loop variables became the language default. A local run in a copy of the captured module creating three snapshots and listing them reported distinct, correctly ordered metadata (index 3, then 2, then 1), so the suspicion is excluded in this toolchain and module combination. The local run is construction knowledge, not retained evidence: no controller execution was performed for it, and the observation is recorded with that limit.
remaining: The aliasing reading depends on the language version applied to the file: the local observation used the same toolchain and go.mod as the run, so it settles the question for this execution environment, but a build with different loop-variable semantics is not covered by it.

feedback.answered: The overview now navigates to the run's confirmed results instead of leaving them only in claim records. formation.explanation: A follower whose heartbeat timer expires while it is an eligible voter transitions to Candidate and runCandidate starts a pre-vote campaign (preElectSelf) that proposes currentTerm+1 without touching the term. Each other voter answers in requestPreVote with the leader-stickiness, membership and log-up-to-date guards and without persisting anything. If a quorum of pre-votes is granted the candidate runs electSelf, which persists the new term and a self-vote, then requests votes; voters persist the vote in requestVote subject to the same guards plus one-vote-per-term. The first tally to reach quorumSize() sets the candidate to Leader. The leader then appends a no-op for its term and replicates; the commitment struct advances commitIndex only when an actual quorum's matchIndex reaches at least startIndex, the first index of the leader's own term.

context.explanation: Authority is the durable current term plus the durable per-term vote; there is no global leader identity. setCurrentTerm persists a term before it is exposed and setState clears the known leader on every transition. A newer term seen in RequestVote or AppendEntries forces a step-down and term update, so context is lost by observation, not by a clock. Leadership transfer pre-replicates to the target and sends TimeoutNow; the target marks candidateFromLeadershipTransfer so that it skips pre-vote and is not stepped down by an equal-term AppendEntries from the outgoing leader, and the flag is cleared after the candidate run. The configuration context is the pair (latest, committed); latest is in effect from the moment its entry is appended.

connection.explanation: The two lines meet in three places. (1) Eligibility for formation is read from the configuration context: only voters of the latest configuration are asked for votes and only their match indexes count for commitment, and the commitment struct is rebuilt from the configuration at leader setup and at each configuration change. (2) The leader's advancement duty is gated by its term context: configurationChangeChIfStable is only non-nil once latest==committed and the leader has committed an entry of its own term (commitIndex >= startIndex), which is why a no-op is dispatched on election even with no client work. (3) Old work is bounded by present authority: a persisted vote is only honoured for its own term, an AppendEntries reply that reports a newer term drives handleStaleTerm and a step-down, a conflicting suffix truncation rolls latest back to committed, and on step-down the leader fails all inflight log futures with ErrLeadershipLost while replication goroutines are stopped.

open_details: appendEntries has an explicit TODO (raft.go:1541): if StoreLogs fails after a truncation, lastLog is left stale. Whether any real store can fail there, and its consequence, is unresolved.
electSelf returns a nil response channel when persisting the self-vote fails (raft.go:2023), leaving the candidate to wait out its election timer; this is a storage-failure path only.

checkLeaderLease assumes leaderState.replState contains every voter of the latest configuration (raft.go:1054); ordering on the main thread appears to guarantee this, but a nil-map lookup would panic and was not tested.

The pre-vote path treats a transport 'unexpected command' error as a granted pre-vote (raft.go:2084-2090), which is intentional for mixed versions but was not analysed for a genuinely unreachable peer.

selections.rationale: Small source-only research product recording a transport-configuration discrepancy: NetworkTransportConfig's InstallSnapshot timeout-scaling comment names a TimeoutScale that the struct does not have, while the constructor always overwrites the transport's own field with the default, so the documented knob is inert. feedback.answered: A further sourced discrepancy was found in the transport configuration surface and recorded as a lead rather than escalated. NetworkTransportConfig documents that 'For InstallSnapshot, we multiply the timeout by (SnapshotSize / TimeoutScale)' (net_transport.go:161-163), but that struct has no TimeoutScale field: the field lives only on the transport itself (net_transport.go:109-110), and NewNetworkTransportWithConfig unconditionally writes DefaultTimeoutScale into it (net_transport.go:226-238), ignoring anything a caller might have expected to configure. So the documented knob for scaling the snapshot send deadline is inert through the public configuration struct, and the only way to change it is to mutate the exported transport field after construction, which the snapshot sender in InstallSnapshot reads directly. The consequence is a tuning gap for slow links or large snapshots rather than a protocol-safety issue, which is why it is recorded as a lead: raising Timeout itself remains an available workaround, though it widens every RPC deadline.
remaining: Whether the ignored knob has ever caused an operational snapshot failure, and whether mutating the exported field is a supported path, are unestablished; the item is a configuration/interface discrepancy with no obligation.

Entry and caller duties: the harness elects a leader, re-establishes an own-term committed entry with a Barrier so configurationChangeChIfStable is open, then drives AddNonvoter on a single-voter cluster where the LogConfiguration entry commits under the existing configuration because nonvoters are excluded from the commitment quorum; no caller duty of the checked premise is skipped. Oracle: the property is evaluated from the emitted fsm_config_delivery event fields (S39 applySingle path is the obligation's implementation site, S36/S37 locate delivery), not from tests_passed, so a process that exits 0 while store_configuration_called stays false is still a violated comparison. Identity: op_id cfg-1 is carried by both the committed prerequisite event and the delivery event. Observation path and completion: the Barrier queued after the configuration entry means the single FIFO fsmMutateCh has been drained through that entry (and index 4 is separately visible in applybatch_config_indices) before the sample is taken; both futures returned nil and the run completed with exit 0. Counterevidence: none of the open issues is evidence against the encoded predicate, and the ApplyBatch statement is recorded below as a limitation rather than as contrary evidence.
